meta.name: Configuring Windows Server Hybrid Advanced Services (AZ-801)
meta.notes: Initial pack — 12 questions across the AZ-801 exam domains: securing Windows Server on-premises and hybrid infrastructures, implementing and managing high availability, disaster recovery, server and workload migration, and monitoring and troubleshooting Windows Server environments. v1.1: +10 — cloud witness, CAU, AD Recycle Bin, repadmin, ASR test failover, Defender for Identity, SMB signing, Azure Update Manager, Windows LAPS, CSV 5120 triage. [scheduled-agent hardening pass 2026-09-07: full-pack rewrite — rebalanced correct-answer positions from A/B/C/D = 13/3/3/3 to 6/5/6/5 with no adjacent runs (sequence B C A D B C A D B C A D C A B D C B A D C A), removed length tells so no correct option is systematically longest or shortest, replaced obviously-fake distractors (Excel-workbook password store, dcdiag placeholder in the CAU question) with plausible near-miss controls, and enriched every explanation with per-distractor reasoning.]

questions.question: Your security team wants domain controllers to refuse to cache the credentials of administrative accounts if they are ever logged on to lower-trust member servers, so that a compromised member server cannot replay or extract those credentials. Which Active Directory feature should you implement to protect privileged accounts in this way?
options: Enable Credential Guard with virtualization-based security on every member server
Make each privileged account a member of the Protected Users global security group
Configure a fine-grained password policy that increases minimum length for administrators
Enable Kerberos armoring (Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling) on every member server
questions.explanation: Membership in the Protected Users global security group hardens accounts at the directory level: NTLM authentication, DES and RC4 encryption in Kerberos, unconstrained delegation, and the caching of plaintext or reversibly-encrypted credentials are all blocked, and Kerberos ticket lifetimes are capped at 4 hours. Credential Guard protects LSA secrets on the local machine using virtualization-based security but does not change what the directory itself hands out to member servers. Fine-grained password policies only alter password length and complexity requirements for a subset of users, not caching behavior. Kerberos armoring (FAST) encrypts the Kerberos pre-authentication exchange but leaves the broader credential-caching surface untouched.

questions.question: A regulated workload running on Windows Server 2022 must be able to run only an explicit allow-list of binaries — including PowerShell scripts and MSI installers — even if an administrator with local privileges attempts to launch an unsigned tool. The policy must be enforced by code integrity at the kernel and user-mode layers, not by a user-space service that an administrator can stop. Which control should you deploy?
options: AppLocker rules enforced through Group Policy
Software Restriction Policies (SRP) applied via GPO
Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) policies
User Account Control (UAC) at the highest prompt level
questions.explanation: Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is enforced by the kernel through the code-integrity subsystem, so a local administrator cannot bypass it by stopping a service — that is its principal advantage over AppLocker, which relies on the AppIDSvc user-mode service and can be disabled by anyone with local admin. Software Restriction Policies (SRP) predate AppLocker and are deprecated on current Windows Server, so Microsoft does not recommend them for new workloads. UAC controls when standard users are prompted to elevate; it does not gate which binaries are allowed to execute at all.

questions.question: You manage roughly 200 on-premises and multi-cloud servers that are connected to Azure with Azure Arc. The compliance team wants Microsoft Defender for Cloud to perform agentless and agent-based threat detection, file integrity monitoring, and vulnerability assessment against those Arc-enabled servers. Which Defender for Cloud plan must be enabled to deliver this coverage on Arc-enabled servers?
options: Microsoft Defender for Servers Plan 2 enabled in Defender for Cloud
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 alone, without a Defender for Cloud plan
Microsoft Defender for Identity with sensors on the domain controllers
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with policy templates for servers
questions.explanation: Defender for Servers Plan 2 is the Defender for Cloud plan that targets servers — Azure VMs and Arc-enabled machines wherever they run — and bundles Defender for Endpoint integration, file integrity monitoring, just-in-time VM access, adaptive application controls, and the integrated vulnerability assessment (formerly Qualys, now Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management). Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 is the EDR product alone; buying it directly does not unlock the Defender for Cloud server-protection surface. Defender for Identity monitors domain controller traffic to detect identity attacks, not general server posture. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS applications and has no server workload coverage.

questions.question: You are designing a 4-node Storage Spaces Direct (S2D) hyper-converged failover cluster that will run virtual machines on Windows Server 2022. The cluster needs to tolerate the loss of any single node and any single drive without losing data or quorum, and the witness must remain available even if the on-premises datacentre WAN is degraded. Which witness configuration best meets these requirements?
options: Configure a disk witness on a shared SAS array attached to all four cluster nodes
Configure a file share witness on a Windows server in the same rack as the cluster
Skip the witness entirely because a 4-node cluster is already inherently even-quorum safe
Configure a cloud witness backed by an Azure storage account in a different region
questions.explanation: An S2D cluster does not use shared SAS storage — each node owns its local drives — so a disk witness is not a supported configuration for S2D. A file share witness co-located in the same rack fails along with the cluster if that rack loses power or its WAN uplink. A 4-node cluster still needs a witness: even-node counts are exactly the split-brain risk quorum is designed to break. A cloud witness uses a tiny arbitration blob in an Azure storage account, has no compute footprint, and remains reachable as long as outbound HTTPS to Azure works — the recommended quorum witness for on-premises clusters that need site-resilient arbitration.

questions.question: Two Windows Server 2022 Hyper-V hosts in different datacentres replicate critical VMs to each other using Hyper-V Replica. Business requirements state that, after a regional outage, you must be able to fail VMs over to the secondary site with a Recovery Point Objective of no more than 30 seconds. Which replication frequency option should you configure for those VMs?
options: 5 minutes
30 seconds
15 minutes
1 hour
questions.explanation: Hyper-V Replica supports exactly three replication intervals: 30 seconds, 5 minutes and 15 minutes. Meeting a 30-second RPO requires the shortest supported interval; anything longer would risk losing more than 30 seconds of writes in an outage. A 1-hour interval is not a supported Hyper-V Replica frequency at all — the setting is not available. For sub-30-second requirements you would move to Storage Replica synchronous replication or an Azure Site Recovery topology with continuous replication, but the question is scoped to Hyper-V Replica.

questions.question: You need to provide crash-consistent, application-consistent, and bare-metal recovery for an on-premises Windows Server 2022 file server, with backups stored off-site in Azure and immutable for 90 days against ransomware and rogue administrators. Which combination should you deploy?
options: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) with an immutable Recovery Services vault
Azure Backup MARS agent with soft delete enabled on the recovery services vault
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering and a 90-day file-version retention policy
A scheduled Robocopy job to an Azure storage account SMB share endpoint
questions.explanation: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) brings application-aware, VSS-based backup of Windows workloads, system state, and bare-metal recovery (BMR), and ships those recovery points to a Recovery Services vault. Enabling vault immutability with a 90-day window (combined with soft delete) protects the recovery points from deletion or modification — even by an operator with Backup admin rights — for the immutability period. The MARS agent alone supports files, folders and system state but does not provide application-aware recovery for workloads like SQL, SharePoint or Exchange. Azure File Sync is a replication tier for hot-cold file storage, not a backup product — deletions on the source propagate to the cloud tier. A Robocopy-to-SMB job is one-way replication with no point-in-time recovery and no immutability layer.

questions.question: You are migrating dozens of file servers from Windows Server 2012 R2 to Windows Server 2022. The migration must preserve NTFS permissions, local users and groups, shares, and the source server's identity (name and IP address) so that clients reconnect transparently, with minimal cutover downtime. Which tool is designed for this scenario?
options: Windows Server Migration Tools (SmigDeploy / Send-SmigServerData)
Distributed File System Replication (DFS-R) with a one-way connection
Storage Migration Service in Windows Admin Center
Robocopy with the /MIR /COPYALL /SECFIX switches
questions.explanation: Storage Migration Service (SMS) in Windows Admin Center was built specifically to inventory, transfer and cut over file servers. It copies files, ACLs, share definitions and local users and groups, and at cutover it can rename the destination and take over the source's IP addresses so clients keep using the same UNC paths without reconfiguration. Windows Server Migration Tools (SmigDeploy / Send-SmigServerData) were retired with older Windows Server versions and never handled identity cutover on modern releases. DFS Replication synchronises a folder's contents between namespaces but never moves shares, local accounts or server identity. Robocopy /MIR /COPYALL /SECFIX transfers file data and ACLs but ignores share definitions, local accounts and the source's identity.

questions.question: Your team must lift-and-shift 60 on-premises VMware virtual machines to Azure with minimal downtime, including dependency analysis and right-sizing recommendations before the move. The migration plane must support agentless replication of the running VMs and a final cutover that boots the workloads as Azure VMs. Which Azure service is purpose-built for this?
options: Azure Site Recovery configured for cross-region Azure-to-Azure disaster recovery
Azure Data Box Heavy shipped for offline bulk data transfer
Azure Resource Mover across subscriptions and regions
Azure Migrate with the Discovery and assessment and Server Migration tools
questions.explanation: Azure Migrate is the unified hub for datacentre migrations: the Discovery and assessment tool inventories VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers and produces Azure readiness and right-sizing reports, and the Server Migration tool performs agentless or agent-based replication of running VMs and a near-zero-downtime cutover into Azure. Azure Site Recovery is a disaster recovery product; it can be used for some migration scenarios but Azure Migrate is the recommended modern path and includes the assessment step this scenario requires. Azure Data Box Heavy ships physical appliances for petabyte-scale offline data transfer — no VM replication or cutover. Azure Resource Mover only moves Azure resources between Azure subscriptions or regions after they are already running in Azure.

questions.question: You want a single Azure pane of glass that ingests performance counters, Windows event logs, and security events from all your Arc-enabled Windows Server 2022 machines into a Log Analytics workspace so that you can query them with Kusto Query Language (KQL). Microsoft has consolidated the legacy MMA and Linux OMS agents into a single supported agent. Which agent should you deploy to those Arc-enabled servers?
options: The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) with Data Collection Rules
The Microsoft Monitoring Agent (MMA / Log Analytics agent)
The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) with a diagnostic setting
The Operations Manager (SCOM) management server agent
questions.explanation: The Azure Monitor Agent (AMA), configured via Data Collection Rules (DCRs), is the supported successor to the legacy Log Analytics agent, MMA and Linux OMS agents. Microsoft has retired the Log Analytics agent for new deployments; AMA is the agent that ships event logs, performance counters, Sysmon and IIS logs into a Log Analytics workspace for KQL queries and Microsoft Sentinel ingestion, and it works on Azure VMs and on Arc-enabled servers alike. The Microsoft Monitoring Agent is precisely the legacy agent that AMA replaces. The Azure Diagnostics extension (WAD) is scoped to older Azure IaaS diagnostics and does not target Arc-enabled machines. A SCOM management server agent reports into an on-premises SCOM management group, not into a Log Analytics workspace.

questions.question: Users intermittently fail to authenticate against a Windows Server 2022 application that uses Kerberos. You suspect duplicate Service Principal Names (SPNs) for the service account. Which built-in command-line tool will list, add, remove, or query duplicate SPNs registered in Active Directory?
options: dcdiag.exe
setspn.exe
nltest.exe
repadmin.exe
questions.explanation: setspn.exe is the supported tool for managing Service Principal Names in Active Directory: setspn -X searches the entire forest for duplicate SPNs (a classic root cause of Kerberos authentication failures), setspn -L lists SPNs for an account and setspn -A / -D add or remove entries. dcdiag runs domain controller health tests but does not enumerate or edit SPNs. nltest queries secure channels, DC discovery and trust state, not SPN records. repadmin diagnoses AD replication convergence between domain controllers and has no SPN operations.

questions.question: You are tightening administrative access to a tier-0 Windows Server 2022 jump host. Operators currently have local Administrators group membership, but auditors require that they only get the specific cmdlets they need to do their job, on demand, with their actions logged and their session run under a temporary virtual account that has no persistent privileges. Which Windows Server feature should you implement?
options: Restricted Groups defined in a Group Policy Object targeting the jump host
Authentication Policies and Authentication Policy Silos scoped to tier-0 admins
Just Enough Administration (JEA) with role capability files and virtual accounts
User Rights Assignment policies denying interactive logon for standard user accounts
questions.explanation: Just Enough Administration (JEA) was designed for exactly this scenario. You define role capability files that whitelist the cmdlets, functions and providers an operator may run, register a constrained PowerShell session configuration, and connections to that endpoint execute under a per-session virtual account that exists only for the lifetime of the session — every command is transcribed and logged. Restricted Groups only enforce membership of local groups; they do not constrain what those members can then run. Authentication Policy Silos restrict where credentials can be presented across the forest, not which cmdlets are exposed inside a session. User Rights Assignment adjusts broad logon rights (interactive, network, batch); it cannot narrow an operator down to a specific command whitelist.

questions.question: Your file server cluster reports the cluster service is degraded and intermittently evicts a node. You need to collect a full cluster log including event-time-correlated entries for every node in a time window, written to a folder you control, for opening a Microsoft support case. Which PowerShell cmdlet collects that diagnostic bundle?
options: Test-Cluster -ReportName ValidationReport
Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Microsoft-Windows-FailoverClustering/Operational'
Show-ClusterPerformanceHistory -ClusterName $env:USERDOMAIN
Get-ClusterLog -Destination C:\Temp -TimeSpan 60
questions.explanation: Get-ClusterLog generates the per-node cluster.log file that Microsoft support engineers expect when diagnosing failover cluster issues — it dumps the in-memory tracing buffer with event-time correlation, and the -Destination and -TimeSpan parameters control where the bundle lands and the window of events included. Test-Cluster runs the cluster validation suite: it is the right tool before deployment or after hardware changes, but it does not collect a runtime log. Get-WinEvent only reads the operational event channel and misses the cluster's in-memory trace buffer. Show-ClusterPerformanceHistory reports S2D performance metrics from the history database, not diagnostics for cluster service failures.

questions.question: A two-node failover cluster spans two sites with no third site available for a file-share witness. Which quorum witness avoids the need for any additional on-premises infrastructure?
options: A disk witness carved from the replicated SAN LUN shared across both sites
Node-majority quorum, which two-node clusters use safely without any witness
A cloud witness using an Azure Storage account as the arbitration point
A USB witness drive attached to the network switch interconnecting the sites
questions.explanation: A cloud witness stores the arbitration blob in an Azure Storage account, giving the cluster a third vote without a third site — the recommended quorum witness for stretch and two-node clusters. A disk witness on replicated SAN storage can split-brain along with the replication itself when the inter-site link fails, since each side may claim the LUN. A two-node cluster running without a witness cannot achieve a majority when either node fails (one out of two is 50%, not a majority). A USB drive shared over the network is not a supported cluster quorum device — the recent USB/file-share-on-router witness support is a specific USB Attached SCSI configuration for edge S2D scenarios with certified hardware, not a generic multi-site cluster witness.

questions.question: Monthly patching of an 8-node Hyper-V cluster is manual: drain a node, patch, reboot, resume, repeat. Which feature automates the whole sequence while keeping workloads online?
options: Cluster-Aware Updating draining, patching, rebooting each node in sequence
Windows Update rings in Intune targeting the cluster host group for staged rollout
Hotpatching every node so the cluster never needs any orchestrated reboots
Scripted live migration triggered by Windows Update's restart-pending flag
questions.explanation: Cluster-Aware Updating (CAU) is purpose-built for this: it places each node in maintenance mode (draining roles via live migration), applies updates, reboots, verifies health, and moves on to the next node — one node at a time, so workloads stay online for the duration of the patch cycle. Windows Update rings in Intune are a client-side patch scheduling feature and do not orchestrate cluster maintenance, drain roles or serialise reboots. Hotpatching (available on Azure Edition and specific Windows Server SKUs) reduces the number of reboots needed for security updates but does not eliminate the orchestration problem, and it does not itself drain nodes or handle non-hotpatched updates. A homegrown script triggered by the restart-pending flag lacks CAU's safety logic — health checks, retry, and per-node serialisation.

questions.question: An administrator accidentally deleted an OU containing 60 user accounts. The AD Recycle Bin was enabled last year. What does recovery look like?
options: Recreate the accounts manually; new SIDs are unavoidable and access must be re-granted
Perform an authoritative restore from a system state backup after booting a DC into DSRM
Restore the OU and its users with Restore-ADObject, attributes and group memberships intact
Reanimate the tombstone objects with LDP.exe, accepting that most attributes and group memberships are lost
questions.explanation: With the AD Recycle Bin enabled, deleted objects retain all attributes (SID, group memberships, distinguished name, populated schema attributes) for the configured deleted-object lifetime, and Restore-ADObject (or the Active Directory Administrative Center) restores them in place — restore the parent OU first, then its children. Recreating accounts by hand produces new SIDs, which invalidates every ACL that referenced the deleted accounts. An authoritative restore from a system state backup with a DC in DSRM is the legacy path the Recycle Bin makes unnecessary for this scenario, and it takes the affected DC offline. Tombstone reanimation with LDP.exe was the pre-Recycle-Bin technique; it works but drops most non-mandatory attributes and group memberships, exactly the loss the Recycle Bin was introduced to prevent.

questions.question: Logons are slow and some GPOs apply inconsistently. You suspect AD replication problems among nine domain controllers. Which command gives the fastest fleet-wide replication health summary?
options: dcdiag /test:dns /dnsbasic against only the PDC emulator FSMO
nltest /dsgetdc:contoso.com from an affected workstation
Get-ADUser -Filter * piped to Measure-Object on each DC
repadmin /replsummary run from a domain controller
questions.explanation: repadmin /replsummary aggregates replication status across every domain controller and produces a compact per-source/per-destination table with largest deltas, failure counts and percentages — the standard first-look tool when replication is suspected. dcdiag /test:dns validates one infrastructure dependency (DNS) on the DC it is run against; it does not measure inter-DC convergence. nltest /dsgetdc reports which DC a specific client chose during locator discovery; it says nothing about whether that DC's data is fresh. Counting AD users with Get-ADUser | Measure-Object reveals nothing about replication delay — two DCs that disagree by minutes on user attributes will still report the same object count.

questions.question: Auditors require proof that the Azure Site Recovery DR plan for on-premises VMs actually works — WITHOUT disrupting production replication or the running workloads. What does ASR provide for this?
options: Planned failover executed during business hours with immediate failback afterwards
Pausing replication during the audit and presenting the vault's replication health report
Test failover, spinning up VM copies from a recovery point in an isolated network
Deleting and re-enabling replication to demonstrate initial seeding completes
questions.explanation: Test failover spins the replicated VMs up in an isolated Azure virtual network from a chosen recovery point — production, ongoing replication and the source workloads are all untouched — then cleans up when you finish, producing exactly the audit evidence required. ASR best-practice guidance is to run test failover on a schedule for precisely this reason. Planned failover is a real cutover: it stops the source workload and transfers ownership to the DR site, which is not audit-only. Pausing replication proves nothing about recoverability and puts the workload out of RPO for the duration. Re-enabling replication tests initial seeding, not the ability to fail over from an existing recovery point.

questions.question: The security team wants detection of identity attacks — Pass-the-Ticket, DCSync, lateral movement reconnaissance — based on domain controller traffic and events. Which Microsoft solution provides these detections?
options: AppLocker policies in audit mode forwarding events to a central collector server
Microsoft Defender for Identity, with sensors installed on the domain controllers
Microsoft Defender Antivirus with cloud-delivered protection set to the High level
Windows Firewall with Advanced Security logging dropped packets on the DC subnet
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Identity places sensors on domain controllers that parse DC network traffic and security events to detect credential-theft tradecraft — DCSync replication abuse, Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket, suspicious LDAP and Kerberos reconnaissance, Golden Ticket usage, lateral movement paths. AppLocker in audit mode records executable launches, not identity-protocol anomalies. Defender Antivirus scans files and behavior on endpoints — it does not model AD authentication traffic. Windows Firewall dropped-packet logging surfaces network activity that hit a deny rule, not the semantics of a Kerberos ticket exchange.

questions.question: A penetration test relayed SMB connections to a file server because clients negotiated unsigned sessions. Which hardening closes SMB relay on Windows Server 2022?
options: Require SMB signing on servers and clients through Group Policy
Move all shares from SMB to NFS with anonymous UID mapping disabled
Restrict SMB to IPv6 so authentication is cryptographically bound
Rename the default administrative shares on every file server
questions.explanation: Relay works because an attacker forwards a client's authentication to a server that accepts unsigned sessions. Mandatory SMB signing (enforced via Group Policy on both server and client sides) makes relayed sessions fail integrity checks because the attacker cannot re-sign packets, and SMB 3.1.1 encryption raises the bar further. Moving to NFS swaps the protocol rather than fixing authentication, and it introduces its own trust model. Restricting SMB to IPv6 does not add cryptographic authentication to the SMB session — IPv6 is a Layer 3 addressing choice, not an auth mechanism. Renaming administrative shares does nothing against relaying because the attacker follows the client's own SMB request; it does not need to guess a share name.

questions.question: 200 on-premises and AWS-hosted Windows servers are Azure Arc-enabled. Compliance needs one view of missing OS updates across all of them, with scheduled patch deployments. Which Azure service delivers this?
options: Microsoft Intune, enrolling each server through the Company Portal application
Azure Policy guest configuration assignments auditing the update agent settings
Windows Server Update Services replicated to one upstream server per environment
Azure Update Manager, assessing and patching Arc-enabled machines alongside Azure VMs
questions.explanation: Azure Update Manager (successor to Automation Update Management) is the Azure-native service for update assessment, one-off and scheduled deployments, and compliance reporting across Azure VMs and Arc-connected machines wherever they run — the single pane the scenario asks for. Intune targets client and mobile endpoints and does not orchestrate server patching at this scale. Azure Policy guest configuration can audit whether settings match a desired state, but it does not deploy updates. WSUS federates update content between sites but does not provide a unified cloud dashboard across Azure Arc-connected servers in AWS or on-premises.

questions.question: Every member server keeps a permanently enabled local Administrator account for break-glass use. Security wants each password unique, rotated automatically, escrowed centrally, with retrieval audited. What is the current Microsoft solution?
options: Windows LAPS escrowing rotated local admin passwords to AD or Entra ID with audited retrieval
A Group Policy Preference pushing one strong local Administrator password to every server
Disabling the local Administrator account and using only domain accounts for break-glass access
A Restricted Groups policy adding a break-glass domain account to every server's local Admins
questions.explanation: Windows LAPS (built into current Windows Server) manages the local Administrator password per machine: it randomises, rotates on schedule, escrows the current password to Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID, gates retrieval by ACL / role assignment with auditing, and rotates immediately after use. A Group Policy Preference that sets an identical Administrator password across every server was the historical anti-pattern LAPS replaced; GPP is deprecated for passwords because the CPassword blob is reversibly encrypted. Disabling the local Administrator account eliminates break-glass entirely — the scenario explicitly requires a break-glass credential. A Restricted Groups policy adding a domain account to local Administrators is a lateral-movement risk in itself and does not solve rotation, escrow or audit.

questions.question: After a SAN firmware update, a CSV-backed Hyper-V cluster logs event 5120 (STATUS_IO_TIMEOUT) and VMs briefly pause during storage path failovers. Which diagnostic sequence is most appropriate FIRST?
options: Convert the CSVs to ReFS immediately, because NTFS cannot recover from I/O timeouts
Check MPIO path state (Get-MPIOStatistics) and SAN fabric logs, then run Validate-Storage
Disable the CSV block cache on every cluster shared volume, since read caching triggers 5120 events
Evict each node in turn and rebuild the cluster from scratch on fresh storage LUNs
questions.explanation: Event 5120 means a CSV lost its direct I/O path to the disk and had to redirect I/O over the network to another owner. After a SAN firmware change the immediate suspects are multipath and fabric — path state, HBA firmware compatibility and switch events. Get-MPIOStatistics surfaces path errors and unbalanced I/O, and the cluster's Validate-Storage tests confirm storage health in a controlled window. Converting the filesystem does not address I/O timeouts; the underlying path failed regardless of NTFS vs ReFS. CSV block cache is a documented performance feature, not a documented cause of 5120 events, so disabling it is treating a symptom that is not tied to the problem. Rebuilding the cluster and re-provisioning storage destroys the diagnostic evidence and incurs downtime for no confirmed root cause.
